strengths: The core idea — applying learnability-driven curriculum design (from DCD/UED) directly to the space of partner policies rather than levels — is a clean and sensible unification, and the framing that prior AHT methods (FCP, MEP, E3T) arise as special cases of a fixed partner generator is illuminating.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: five Overcooked-AI layouts, strong population-based (FCP, MEP) and population-free (SP, E3T) baselines with documented fairness measures (larger populations, extended training, per-layout LR tuning for baselines), two ablations, a comparison of four learnability functions, a joint UED setting (JUPD on the OGC), and a double-blind human user study with ethics approval, Holm-Bonferroni correction, and reliability analysis (Cronbach's alpha).

UPD works with a single hyperparameter set across all layouts while baselines required per-layout tuning, supporting the 'no manual tuning' claim, and Fig. 3 gives concrete evidence that the curriculum adapts epsilon per layout as intended.

The ablation structure is informative: UPD w/o ℓ remains competitive, and the learnability-function comparison (Fig. 5) shows the method is robust to the specific scoring choice, with the interesting negative result that complex UED learnability functions give no benefit for partner selection.

Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameter tables, search ranges, compute requirements (single 16GB GPU), and a clear reproducibility statement; the limitations section is honest about discrete actions, narrow behavioural diversity, and agent-agent vs human evaluation gaps.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: UPD is essentially E3T with (i) epsilon sampled uniformly instead of fixed, (ii) a Dirichlet bias mask on the random policy, and (iii) a variance-based buffer selection borrowed from SFL (Rutherford et al. 2024) / Monette et al. (2025). Each ingredient is individually well-precedented; the contribution is their composition and the empirical demonstration.

Evaluation is confined to a single environment family: Overcooked-AI and the OGC are both Overcooked. The broad claims about 'robust ad-hoc teamwork' and a 'general framework for partner generation' rest entirely on one domain, and no evidence is provided that the variance-based learnability signal transfers to other cooperative tasks (e.g., Hanabi, GRF, or even other Overcooked variants with different reward structures).

The variance-based learnability score has a confound the paper does not fully address: return variance under (π_ego, π_p) is driven partly by partner stochasticity (biased random policies are inherently noisy) rather than solely by the ego agent being at its learning frontier. The authors' own motivation (variance highest when half of returns are 0 and half Rmax) is contradicted by their finding that agents 'rarely score zero reward', making the theoretical grounding loose; robustness across scoring functions (Fig. 5) mitigates but does not resolve this.

Statistical support for the headline claims is thin: Table 1 reports mean ± std over six seeds, but no significance tests or confidence intervals are given for the artificial-agent comparisons, and the margin between full UPD and UPD w/o ℓ (94.4 vs 90.0, with stds of ~8-11) may not be reliable — this matters because learnability selection is one of the paper's central claims.

The 'first method enabling fully unsupervised curricula over both level and partner distributions' and 'first approach that unifies AHT and UED' claims need careful qualification given concurrent/nearby open-ended AHT work (e.g., ROTATE, Wang et al. 2025, which they cite as growing populations); the boundary between 'growing populations' and 'population-free' could be contested by reviewers of that work.

The human study, while methodologically careful, is small (12 participants, 36 games per method), and the emergent 'convention-breaking' finding (Fig. 4) is acknowledged as a hypothesis ('We hypothesise this increases return variance...') yet is highlighted as a key emergent phenomenon in the discussion.

Several presentation issues: the JUPD learnability switch from ℓ_var to ℓ_CV² is motivated in one sentence with limited analysis of when normalization matters; Figure 14's legend mislabels SFL-E3T as 'SF-LE3T'; and per-partner results (Fig. 18) show UPD is slightly outperformed by MEP on some partners, which is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The core idea — applying learnability-driven curriculum selection (SFL-style) directly to the partner-policy space rather than the level space, using stochastic mixtures of the ego policy — is clean, lightweight, and well-motivated, and the framing of prior AHT methods (FCP, MEP, E3T) as special cases with fixed generators/populations is a useful conceptual contribution.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: population-based (FCP, MEP) and population-free (E3T, SP) baselines across five Overcooked layouts, a learnability-function comparison (Fig. 5), a joint partner+environment variant (JUPD) on the OGC benchmark (Table 2), extensive appendix analyses of curriculum dynamics (Figs. 15-17), and a double-blind human user study with reasonable statistical hygiene (Holm-Bonferroni corrections, Cronbach's alpha, ethics approval).

The paper is transparent about fairness in baseline comparisons (larger populations, extended best-response training, per-layout learning-rate tuning for FCP/MEP) and provides detailed hyperparameter tables and ranges, supporting reproducibility.

Emergent phenomena such as the epsilon-scheduling behaviour (Fig. 3) and symmetry-breaking biases (Fig. 4) are interesting qualitative findings, and the appendix analysis (Sec. F, H) honestly probes why hard-partner prioritisation fails in an open-ended generator.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: UPD is essentially E3T's mixture generator plus an SFL-style variance curator plus Dirichlet bias masking. The learnability score (return variance, Eq. 4) is a simple statistic, and the ablation shows the selection criterion contributes relatively little: UPD w/o ℓ reaches 90.0 vs. 94.4 average return (Table 1), so a large part of the gain comes from stochastic online generation rather than the adaptive curriculum that is the paper's central claim.

Evaluation is confined to the Overcooked family (Overcooked-AI and a 5x5 OGC variant). Generalisation claims about 'robust ad-hoc teamwork' would be far more convincing with at least one additional domain (e.g., Hanabi, a gridworld AHT suite, or human-model evaluations outside the authors' own construction).

The evaluation populations are designed by the authors from a small number of hard-coded, planning, and BRDiv agents (4-9 per layout), which risks biasing comparisons; no external standard population (e.g., the Carroll et al. human-model pool) is used.

The human study is small (12 participants, 144 games) and limited to three layouts; while statistically corrected, the effect-size support for headline claims of 'significantly more adaptive, more human-like' is thin at this N.

A closely related concurrent/regret-driven method, ROTATE (Wang et al. 2025), is cited but not empirically compared against, despite being the most directly relevant open-ended AHT training baseline; the 'first method enabling fully unsupervised curricula over level and partner distributions' claim is asserted rather than rigorously delimited against it.

The variance-based score is susceptible to degenerate incentives: partners whose behaviour induces high return variance (including intentionally destabilising partners, as the authors' own convention-breaking analysis hints) may be selected for variance rather than pedagogical value. The paper offers a hypothesis (Sec. on Fig. 4) but no controlled evidence that the selected curricula are causally beneficial beyond the ablation.

Minor presentation issues reduce polish: Figure 8's caption mislabels the layout order ('CR, AA, CR, CC and FC'), Figure 14's legend says 'three methods' for four curves, and key implementation choices (buffer refresh, N, K interplay) are spread across the main text and appendix, making the full training procedure harder to reconstruct than it should be.

Computational cost of the learnability scoring loop (N=10 rollouts per candidate partner, 8192 generated agents, buffer refresh) is not quantified relative to baselines, which weakens the 'lightweight' framing.

strengths: The central idea is clear and well-motivated: applying dual curriculum design / learnability-based selection to the partner policy space rather than the environment space, yielding a population-free AHT method. The framing that FCP, MEP, and E3T are special cases of a fixed partner generator is insightful and helps unify the AHT literature.

The proposed method is genuinely lightweight (Alg. 1-3): partner generation via uniform epsilon mixing plus Dirichlet bias masks, scored by return variance, adds minimal computational overhead and requires no pretrained populations or task-specific tuning of the mixture coefficient, which is a practical improvement over E3T.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: five Overcooked layouts with six seeds, a diverse evaluation population (BRDiv agents, planning agents, hardcoded agents, worst-case agents), tuned baselines (including extra compute for FCP/MEP best-response training), component ablations, a comparison of four learnability functions, a joint partner-environment variant (JUPD) on the OGC, and a double-blind human user study.

The human study (Section 5.3, Appendix I) is a significant strength: within-subjects design, double-blind protocol, IRB approval, corrected statistical tests, and Cronbach's alpha for the aggregated preference score. It directly addresses the paper's own point that agent-agent evaluations do not reliably predict human-AI alignment.

Analysis beyond raw scores is valuable: Figure 3 shows the curriculum adapts epsilon per layout, Figure 4 documents emergent convention-breaking dynamics, Appendix F shows learnability concentrates on intermediate-difficulty partners, and Appendix H explains why prioritizing hardest partners collapses in an open-ended generator setting.

Reproducibility is good: full hyperparameter tables (Tables 3-4), search spaces, compute details, and a code availability statement; the method itself is simple enough to reimplement from the algorithms as written.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to the Overcooked family (Overcooked-AI and a 5x5 OGC variant). Both RQ1 and RQ4 are effectively tested on one domain, and the OGC experiments use a reduced-size version of the benchmark. Evidence for the generality of UPD beyond this domain is absent, which limits the strength of the 'general framework' claim.

Conceptual novelty is moderate: the method is a careful combination of existing pieces - E3T's ego/random policy mixture, SFL's learnability-based selection, a return-variance score related to Monette et al., and Dirichlet bias sampling similar in spirit to prior human-bias modeling (Yu et al. 2023). The primary novelty is the joint application and the adaptivity of epsilon, not a fundamentally new mechanism. This is acknowledged but should temper enthusiasm.

Statistical support for the artificial-agent results is incomplete: only six seeds are used, per-layout standard deviations are large, and on some layouts (e.g., CC) the full method ties or is within noise of the ablations. No significance testing is reported for Table 1 or Table 2, unlike the careful statistics applied to the human study.

Hyperparameters were selected using a BRDiv evaluation population as a 'cheap proxy' (Appendix C). Since that population is part of the evaluation distribution used in Table 1, there is a risk of optimistically biasing the comparison, even though baselines were also tuned to some degree.

Some interpretive claims are speculative: the emergent convention-breaking in Figure 4 is offered as a hypothesis without a controlled experiment isolating the mechanism, and the argument that variance-based scoring prepares agents for 'best- and worst-case partners' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The ablation gap is partly ambiguous: UPD w/o l (no learnability scoring) performs nearly as well (90.0 vs 94.4 average), which weakens the evidence that adaptive selection - the paper's headline contribution - is the main driver of the gains relative to simply randomizing epsilon.
The human study, while methodologically careful, involves only 12 participants and 36 games per method, so the significance claims about human preference rest on a small sample.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: UPD extends learnability-driven UED (SFL) from environment parameters to partner policies, yielding a population-free AHT method that removes both pre-trained partner populations and E3T's fixed, hand-tuned mixing coefficient.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 282 trained policies across LBF, five Overcooked-AI layouts, and the OGC benchmark; strong and competitively tuned baselines (SP, FCP with 48-agent populations, MEP with enlarged/tuned populations, E3T, and ROTATE in the appendix); ablations (UPD w/o bias, UPD w/o ℓ, fine-tuned UPD); and useful mechanistic analyses (Figures 4-6 on ε selection, learnability-return scatter plots, and emergent convention-breaking).

A double-blind human study with ethics approval, Holm-Bonferroni-corrected statistics, and appropriate hedging about sample size (n=12) strengthens the central claim beyond artificial partners, which are the norm in this literature.

Reproducibility is good: full hyperparameter tables, search spaces (Tables 4-7), a computational cost analysis with a break-even population size derivation (Appendix F), and an honest transparency note acknowledging that earlier baseline configurations had issues that were corrected.

The paper is candid about limitations: the appendix shows ROTATE outperforms UPD on 3 of 5 layouts, the ablation showing most gains come from large-scale generation/biasing rather than learnability scoring is reported openly, and the discussion correctly notes UPD shifts rather than eliminates computation.
weaknesses: The contribution of the headline mechanism (learnability scoring) is modest: UPD w/o ℓ achieves 90.8 average vs 94.4 for full UPD in Table 1, so most of the improvement over E3T comes from randomized ε and the Dirichlet bias mechanism rather than the variance-based curriculum. The paper's own analysis supports this interpretation, which weakens the centrality of the 'learnability-based partner design' claim, even though the resulting method works well.

The theoretical justification is indirect and heuristic: the appeal to Foster et al. (2026) concerns expected one-step improvement under standard policy gradient settings; applying it to a buffered, partner-induced game with off-policy-style selection is not formally established, and no proof or assumptions analysis is provided for the AHT setting.

Novelty is incremental relative to E3T: the method is essentially E3T with stochastically sampled ε, Dirichlet action-bias masks, and a variance-based filter inherited from SFL. The extension to joint partner-environment curricula (JUPD) is a natural composition rather than a new algorithmic idea, and is only evaluated on a reduced 5×5 OGC variant.

The comparison against ROTATE, arguably the strongest recent open-ended AHT method, appears only in the appendix with 3 seeds (vs 6 elsewhere), while the main text results tables omit it; given ROTATE beats UPD on the majority of layouts, this comparison deserves more prominence and statistical care.

Evaluation partners are generated largely with the same pipelines (BRDiv, Wang et al. 2025 generators) used in training-adjacent baselines, which could subtly favor methods tuned to that generator family; the human study partially mitigates but is small.

Minor presentation issues: the project page URL in the reproducibility statement is blank, Figure 1's 'Learnability?' framing oversells the scoring criterion given the ablation results, and the citation to Foster et al. (2026) references a venue that postdates the submission, making the key theoretical anchor unverifiable at review time.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: extending learnability-driven curricula (SFL) from environment/level space to partner policy space is a natural, principled way to make population-free ad-hoc teamwork training adaptive, and the induced single-agent game formalism (Eqs. 2-4) makes this extension precise.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: results span LBF, five Overcooked-AI layouts with strong population-based (FCP, MEP) and population-free (E3T, ROTATE) baselines, the OGC procedural benchmark, and a double-blind within-subjects human study (144 games, corrected Wilcoxon/t-tests, ethics approval). The claim of evaluating 282 trained policies reflects genuine scale.

Honest and revealing ablations: the paper openly reports that UPD w/o ℓ achieves most of the gain (90.8 vs 94.4 average), correctly attributing much of the improvement to large-scale partner generation and biasing rather than learnability scoring alone, and discusses this implication rather than hiding it.

Good mechanistic analysis: Figures 4-6 show layout-dependent ε selection, intermediate-difficulty partner selection, and emergent convention-breaking dynamics, with the Appendix C matrix-game example explaining why variance-based scoring discourages convention overfitting.

Appendix F provides a quantitative computational cost analysis with a break-even population size, and the paper is candid about when UPD's tradeoffs may not be favourable (expensive simulators), as well as including a transparency note about earlier baseline configuration issues.

A single UPD hyperparameter configuration works across all Overcooked layouts, in contrast to per-layout tuning needed for E3T, MEP, and (fine-tuned) baselines — supporting the central 'removing manual tuning' claim.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially E3T with ε~U(0,1), a Dirichlet bias mask, and a variance-based buffer borrowed from SFL. The theoretical justification (proportionality of expected improvement to advantage-signal variance) is imported wholesale from Foster et al. and applied by analogy to induced games, without any new formal guarantees for the actual algorithm (buffering, top-|B| selection, PPO).

The learnability mechanism — the paper's titular contribution — contributes a comparatively small margin over random partner generation (94.4±2.3 vs 90.8±6.0, overlapping error bars), and the method loses to plain self-play on CRoom. In the appendix, ROTATE outperforms UPD on 3 of 5 layouts, and UPD only wins on average after per-layout fine-tuning (102.3±0.6), which somewhat undercuts the 'no tuning needed' narrative.

The OGC experiment uses a reduced 5×5 version of the benchmark, so the strongest scaling claim (joint partner-environment curricula) is demonstrated only on a simplified variant, with only three evaluation layouts and a small set of adapted baselines.

The human study has only 12 participants; while the statistics are appropriately corrected and the authors acknowledge the sample-size limitation, the human-preference conclusions rest on a thin evidence base.

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete reproducibility statement: the project page URL is blank, and no code release is confirmed despite the paper's reliance on specific in-house modifications to JaxMARL, Jumanji-LBF, and E3T/FCP/MEP codebases.

Reference hygiene issues, e.g. citing Foster et al. '2026' (NeurIPS 2026, a future venue) as a key theoretical foundation, and hyperparameter tables reveal that many curriculum parameters (buffer size, N, R) have nontrivial sensitivity, only partially explored.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed contribution: extending learnability-driven UED (SFL) from environment levels to partner policies is a natural yet non-obvious idea, and the paper articulates the 'induced training environment' formalism (Eq. 2-4) cleanly, making the conceptual bridge to UED rigorous.

Strong and broad empirical evaluation: 282 trained policies across LBF, five Overcooked-AI layouts, and the procedurally generated OGC; comparisons against both population-based (FCP, MEP, ROTATE) and population-free (SP, E3T) baselines with competitive, often stronger, results (e.g., +18% over E3T on Overcooked-AI average, best average on OGC).

Rare and valuable human-AI user study (double-blind, within-subjects, ethics-board approved, Holm-Bonferroni corrected statistics, Cronbach's alpha reported) showing higher returns and subjective preference for UPD; claims are appropriately hedged given the sample size.

Thorough mechanistic analysis that supports the method's story: learnability concentrates on intermediate-difficulty partners (Fig. 5, App. I), adaptive epsilon selection differs across layouts and time (Fig. 4), and emergent convention-breaking dynamics arise without explicit mechanisms (Fig. 6), backed by ablations (App. J.1.2) showing these dynamics require the interaction of generation and learnability filtering.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper openly reports that UPD w/o learnability performs nearly as well, that learnability gains are layout-dependent, and includes a transparency note about corrected baseline configuration issues. Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameters, seed counts, compute analysis (App. F), and code provenance are provided.

Theoretical grounding is at least sketched: the connection between return variance and expected policy improvement via Foster et al., plus the 2x2 coordination game analysis of convention selection (Sec. 4.4, App. C), gives principled intuition for why variance-based selection discourages convention overfitting.
weaknesses: The method is arguably incremental: it combines E3T-style partner generation with SFL-style variance scoring plus a Dirichlet bias mask. The empirical ablation shows UPD w/o learnability scoring achieves +14.1% versus +18.0% for the full method, so the headline mechanism contributes a modest fraction of the gain; the paper acknowledges this but the contribution then rests partly on large-scale generation, which is closer to domain randomization over partners.

The theoretical justification is informal: the Foster et al. result concerns variance of the advantage/learning signal under policy gradient methods, and its application to trajectory return variance in the induced single-agent game is a heuristic leap rather than a proven statement; no formal guarantee is given for when prioritizing high-variance partners improves learning.

The human study, while well-designed, is small (12 participants, 36 games per method) and limited to three layouts; conclusions about human-AI collaboration quality are necessarily preliminary, and the paper appropriately qualifies them but the abstract phrasing is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants.

The OGC evaluation uses a reduced 5x5 version of the benchmark, and evaluation partners are largely synthetic/handcrafted or BRDiv agents; evidence of transfer to genuinely human-like partner distributions outside the user study is limited.

Some comparisons use only 3 seeds (ROTATE, fine-tuned UPD in Table 3) and error bars sometimes overlap, so the claim that UPD outperforms ROTATE in aggregate should be read cautiously; the project page link in the reproducibility statement appears to be missing/blank.
The paper cites a NeurIPS 2026 reference (Foster et al.) that appears to be concurrent/unpublished, making the central theoretical claim difficult to verify at review time.
